videos.script: In 1960, a phone call from London to New York did something that sounds absurd now: the network reserved a path. A real circuit, end to end, held open for you and unusable by anybody else, for as long as you talked. {{circuit}} The internet reserves nothing. There is no line held open between you and the machine you are reading this from, and there never was. So how does the message get there at all? {{nothing-reserved}} It gets cut up. Your message is chopped into pieces. Every piece is given the address of where it is going. And every piece is put into the network to find its own way there. {{cut-up}} That is a packet, and it is the single idea this entire lesson is built on. The frame, the socket, the handshake — every one of them is a consequence of the network having no line to hold open for you. By the end you will be able to say what a packet carries, where it stops, how it crosses a network it does not belong to, and why a video call and a file download are built on opposite trades. {{title}}

You have read that TCP gives you order and delivery, and that UDP gives you neither. What that costs is easiest to see on a clock. {{clock}} Here is a browser on the left and a server on the right, and the distance between them is a hundred and fifty milliseconds. That number is not a bad connection. It is most of the way across an ocean, and no amount of bandwidth reduces it. {{distance}} The browser wants to send one request. Before a single byte of that request leaves, it sends this: a SYN. One small packet that says, I would like to open a connection, and here is the number I will start counting my bytes from. {{syn}} A hundred and fifty milliseconds later it arrives. The server answers with a SYN-ACK: I accept, here is my own starting number, and I acknowledge yours. {{syn-ack}} Another hundred and fifty milliseconds, and the browser has it. It sends the ACK — agreed — and it can finally send the request along with it. {{ack}} Look at the clock. Three hundred milliseconds have gone by and the server has not yet seen a single byte of what was actually being asked for. That is the price, and it is paid once per connection, before the work starts. {{cost}} Now watch what UDP does instead. {{wipe}} The first packet is the data. There is no agreement, because there is nothing to agree about: nobody is going to count these, nobody is going to resend them, and nobody is going to hold one back to wait for the one in front of it. {{udp}} That is the whole trade, on one clock. TCP spends a round trip to buy you a numbered, acknowledged, ordered stream. UDP spends nothing and gives you none of it. Neither is better. A file needs every byte and can wait; a voice call needs the next twenty milliseconds and would rather lose a syllable than wait for it. {{trade}}
